metric.why: Annual matching and hourly matching are very different claims; hourly carbon-free matching is the harder standard the largest operators now report progress against. Reading which claim is being made matters more than the percentage.
metric.definition: The share of facility consumption matched by renewable generation, reported either as annual matching through purchased certificates or as around-the-clock hourly matching.

reading.body:
How a data center reports renewable energy matters more than the percentage itself, because annual matching through certificates and hourly matching are fundamentally different claims about carbon-free operations.

The largest operators now distinguish between annual matching, where purchased certificates offset yearly consumption in aggregate, and hourly matching, where renewable generation covers demand at each moment of operation. Hourly matching is the harder standard and the one increasingly used in public disclosures by major players. This distinction matters because it reveals whether a facility actually runs on renewable power when it operates or simply purchases offsets that may not align with the timing of consumption.

For AI infrastructure, this distinction directly affects grid stress and power procurement strategy. A data center claiming annual matching might draw coal power at peak hours while banking renewable credits from times of surplus generation. Hourly matching requires either on-site renewable capacity, battery storage, or grid contracts that supply power at the exact hours needed. As AI facilities scale and concentrate demand, the difference between these claims translates into real constraints on where and how data centers can expand without destabilizing regional grids.

The metric does not capture total carbon footprint, water usage, or heat dissipation. It also does not measure whether purchased certificates represent new renewable capacity or existing generation simply reassigned through the market. A facility with high hourly matching may still import power from distant sources or rely on storage systems with their own efficiency losses.
